title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Texas Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing, and Order Granting Accelerated Approval of, a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 17.111(d) (Commodity-Based Trust Shares)
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Texas Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing, and Order Granting Accelerated Approval of, a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 17.111(d) (Commodity-Based Trust Shares)

1. Purpose TXSE Rule 17.111(d) currently governs the listing and trading of Commodity-Based Trust Shares on the Exchange. Under the existing rule, the Exchange is required to submit a separate proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act before listing Commodity-Based Trust Shares. The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 17.111(d) to establish generic listing standards that would permit the Exchange to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that satisfy the requirements of Rule 17.111(d) pursuant to Rule 19b-4(e) under the Act. Commodity-Based Trust Shares that do not satisfy the applicable generic listing standards could continue to be listed pursuant to a separate proposed rule change under Section 19(b) of the Act. Background The proposed standards are substantially similar to generic listing standards previously approved by the Commission for Nasdaq, Cboe BZX, and NYSE Arca. In July 2026, the Commission approved amendments to Nasdaq's generic listing standards that, among other things, permit up to 15% of the net asset value (``NAV'') of a Trust's holdings to consist of certain digital commodities and securities that do not otherwise satisfy the applicable generic eligibility criteria, add a definition of ``digital commodity,'' and permit actively managed Commodity-Based Trust Shares, subject to additional safeguards. The Commission subsequently approved substantially similar amendments for NYSE Arca and Cboe BZX and materially identical amendments for Nasdaq Texas. The Exchange's proposal incorporates both the original generic listing standards and the subsequent amendments into Rule 17.111(d), with changes necessary to conform the Exchange's existing rule structure, definitions, and cross-references. Proposal The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 17.111(d) to permit the Exchange to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that satisfy the requirements of Rule 17.111(d) pursuant to Rule 19b-4(e) under the Act. Rule 19b-4(e) provides that the listing and trading of a new derivative securities product by a self-regulatory organization is not deemed a proposed rule change pursuant to Rule 19b-4(c)(1) if the Commission has approved, pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act, the self-regulatory organization's trading rules, procedures, and listing standards for the product class that would include the new derivative securities product and the self-regulatory organization has a surveillance program for the product class. Consistent with the Commission-approved generic listing standards, the Exchange would retain the ability to submit a proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that do not satisfy one or more of the applicable generic listing standards. The proposed rule would also provide that statements or representations contained in any such proposed rule change concerning (1) the description of the index, Trust holdings, or reference assets; (2) limitations on the index, Trust holdings, or reference assets; (3) the dissemination and availability of the index, Trust holdings, reference assets, or Intraday Indicative Values; or (4) the applicability of Exchange listing rules would constitute continued listing requirements. An issuer would be required to notify the Exchange of any failure to comply with such continued listing requirements. If the Commodity-Based Trust Shares do not satisfy those requirements, the Exchange may suspend trading and will initiate delisting proceedings under the TXSE Rule Series 16.500. Definitions The Exchange also proposes to modernize the definition of Commodity-Based Trust Shares in renumbered Rule 17.111(d)(3). As proposed, Commodity-Based Trust Shares could be issued by a trust, limited liability company, partnership, or other similar entity that, if applicable, is operated by a registered commodity pool operator pursuant to the Commodity Exchange Act and is not registered as an investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940, or a series or class thereof. Consistent with its stated investment objective and policies, a Trust could hold one or more commodities or commodity-based assets and, in addition, securities, cash and cash equivalents. The proposed rule would also retain the existing creation and redemption structure, as expanded to accommodate the broader range of permitted holdings and cash creations and redemptions based on the next determined NAV per Trust share. The Exchange also proposes to amend the definition of ``commodity'' in Rule 17.111(d)(3)(B) to provide that the term is defined in Section 1a(9) of the Commodity Exchange Act and does not include an ``excluded commodity'' as defined in Section 1a(19) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(C) would define the term ``commodity- based asset'' as any future, option, or swap on a commodity, as defined in proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(B). Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(D) would define the term ``digital commodity'' as a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(E) would define the term ``cash equivalent'' as a short-term instrument with a maturity of less than three months consisting of: (1) U.S. Government securities, including bills, notes, and bonds differing as to maturity and rates of interest, that are either issued or guaranteed by the U.S. Treasury or by U.S. Government agencies or instrumentalities; (2) certificates of deposit issued against funds deposited in a bank or savings and loan association; (3) bankers' acceptances; (4) repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements; (5) bank time deposits; (6) commercial paper; and (7) money market funds. raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq Texas, LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposal To Amend Equity 4, Rule 4120, To Align It With That of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC

1. Purpose When in September of this year the Exchange updated its rulebook at Equity 1 and Equity 4 to more closely align those rules with the equivalent rules of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (``Nasdaq''), in anticipation of the Exchange becoming a primary listing venue in 2027, the Exchange mistakenly copied an obsolete version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. The Commission had approved the current version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, back in 2022. However, this version of the rule did not become operative until August of this year. This delay in making the 2022 changes operative on Nasdaq led to the Exchange mistakenly copying in its September 2026 filing an obsolete version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. The Exchange proposes to correct this mistake in this filing. The Exchange proposes to replace in its entirety its current version of Equity 4, Rule 4120, with the version of that rule that is currently found in the Nasdaq rulebook. Therefore, the new version of Nasdaq Texas Equity 4, Rule 4120, would be structured as follows: 1. Section (a) (Definitions) defines certain terms that are used in the rule. 2. Section (b) (Regulatory Halts) establishes the Exchange's authority to initiate regulatory halts or pauses in various circumstances, including: halts provided for by the applicable SIP Plan; discretionary Regulatory Halts relating to issuer information, material news, initial public offerings, index warrants, derivative securities products, foreign securities, market disruptions, and Initial ETP Opens; and mandatory Regulatory Halts relating to dissemination issues for derivative securities products, the Limit Up- Limit Down Mechanism, market-wide circuit breakers, Equity Investment Tracking Stocks and Subscription Receipts, and reverse stock splits. 3. Section (c) (Operational Halts) establishes the Exchange's authority and procedures for initiating and terminating Operational Halts, including: the circumstances in which Nasdaq Texas may declare an Operational Halt, notification to the SIP when Nasdaq Texas has concerns about collecting and transmitting quotation or transaction information or has declared an Operational Halt or suspension, and the procedures for resuming trading when Nasdaq Texas determines that trading may resume in a fair and orderly manner. The changes that the Exchange would make to the Nasdaq rule to tailor it to the Exchange would be the following: 1. Modify references to the operating hours and trading sessions of the Exchange, so that they correctly reflect those of Nasdaq Texas. This includes not carrying over language in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, that pertains to Nasdaq's upcoming transition to trading 23 hours a day, 5 days a week. 2. Eliminate references to a direct listing with capital raise, as that option is not present in the Nasdaq Texas rulebook. 3. Update references to ``Nasdaq'' with ``Nasdaq Texas.'' Additionally, the Exchange will not copy references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol that are currently present in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. This is because the Exchange, Nasdaq, and Nasdaq PHLX LLC will be imminently submitting separate filings to abandon their plans to deploy the CORE FIX order entry protocol, due to a lack of interest by exchange participants. Therefore, it makes no sense for the Exchange to copy references to CORE FIX in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, that will soon become obsolete. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system by aligning the Exchange's rulebook at Equity 4, Rule 4120, with the substantially similar rule of Nasdaq, which was previously approved by the Commission, finding it to be consistent with the Act. The proposal is also consistent with Section 6(b)(5) because it is designed to promote clarity, consistency, and transparency for Participants, issuers, and market participants by replacing stale rule text with the version of Equity 4, Rule 4120, that reflects the Commission-approved Nasdaq framework and the intervening updates already incorporated into Nasdaq's current operative rule. The Commission previously approved Nasdaq's Rule 4120 framework to add categories of regulatory and operational halts, reorganize Rule 4120, incorporate provisions of the applicable equity data plans, and make conforming changes to related rules. In approving that framework, the Commission recognized that the revisions promote a clear and uniform approach to trading halts, improve coordination and certainty among plan participants and market participants, enhance the resiliency and integrity of market systems, and promote fair and orderly markets and investor protection. Nasdaq Texas's proposal advances those same objectives because it would adopt a substantially similar halt framework while tailoring only the exchange name, trading session terminology, and other conforming elements needed to reflect the Exchange's existing rules and operations. The Exchange therefore believes the proposal will reduce confusion, support consistent cross- market halt and resumption procedures, and help Participants understand when the Exchange may halt, pause, or resume trading and how related rules will operate. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Exchange Rule 2(c)
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Exchange Rule 2(c)

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 2 (``Member,'' ``Membership,'' ``Member Firm,'' etc.) to restore language inadvertently omitted from the proposed definition of ``associated person'' in a recent rule filing. More specifically, the proposed change is a technical amendment that would ensure that the persons encompassed by the ``approved person'' category that the Exchange recently filed to delete are captured by the definition of ``associated person'' in Rule 2(c) for jurisdictional and all other applicable Exchange rules. The proposed rule change is not intended to effect any substantive change to the scope of the Exchange's jurisdiction. Background and Proposed Rule Change On September 18, 2026, the Exchange filed an immediately effective rule change to (1) eliminate the ``approved person'' registration category as no longer necessary, (2) adopt a new definition of ``associated person'' in Rule 2(c) based on the definition of associated person in Rule 1011(b) of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (``FINRA'') and elements of the current definition of approved person, and (3) make related technical and conforming changes. The Approved Person Filing is scheduled to become operative on October 18, 2026. As described in the Approved Person Filing, the Exchange did not intend to expand or narrow the scope of its jurisdiction. Rather, the proposal was designed to ensure that all persons currently encompassed by the approved person category would continue to be covered under the proposed definition of ``associated person.'' Specifically, the filing stated that proposed Rule 2(c)(3) would include the existing categories of approved persons: (i) persons that control a member organization; (ii) persons engaged in a securities or kindred business that is controlled by a member or member organization; and (iii) U.S. registered broker-dealers under common control with a member organization. The filing further explained that the proposed definition of ``Control Person'' was intended to encompass those same categories. The Exchange has since determined that the text of proposed Rule 2(c)(3), as filed, inadvertently omitted the clause covering persons engaged in a securities or kindred business that is controlled by a member or member organization. That clause appears in the Exchange's current approved person definition and was intended to be carried forward without substantive change. Consequently, the text of proposed Rule 2(c)(3) is inconsistent with both the description of the proposal and the Exchange's stated intent in the Approved Person Filing, which was to preserve, rather than modify, the existing scope of Exchange jurisdiction. This proposed rule change corrects that inadvertent omission and conforms the rule text to the proposal as described in the Approved Person Filing. The Exchange accordingly proposes to amend Rule 2(c)(3) to add the phrase ``a person engaged in a securities or kindred business that is controlled by a member or member organization,'' immediately after ``controlled by a member organization,''. Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Introduce Enhancements to the Missed Liquidity Report Offered as Part of the Cboe Timestamping Service

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes introduce enhancements to the Cboe Timestamping Service, which is a market data service comprised of the Missed Liquidity Report, Missed Cancels Report and All Cancels Report. Specifically, the Exchange seeks to update the Missed Liquidity Report to now include Complex Order Auction (``COA'') and Complex Automated Improvement Mechanism (``C-AIM'') events (collectively, ``Auction Orders'' or an ``Auction''), as well as a new price field that, for records related to Auction Orders, includes each price of the subscribing Member's orders, modify messages, and quotes, as well as each price level at which options orders were executed during an Auction. The Exchange is not proposing any enhancements to either the Missed Cancels Report or the All Cancels Report. Background Currently, the Cboe Timestamping Service provides timestamp information for orders, quotes and cancels for market participants. More specifically, the Cboe Timestamping Service reports provide various timestamps relating to the message lifecycle throughout the Exchange System. The reports are optional products that are available to all Members and Members may opt to choose any combination of reports or no reports at all. Corresponding fees are assessed based on the number of reports selected. Notably, the data included in these reports is based only on the data of the market participant that opts to subscribe to the reports (``Recipient Member'') and does not include information related to any Member other than the Recipient Member. The Exchange restricts all other market participants from receiving another market participant's data. Additionally, no report includes real-time market data. Rather, the reports contain only historical data from the prior trading day and are only available after the end of the trading day, generally on a T+1 basis. Specifically, the Missed Liquidity Report provides time details for executions of orders and quotes that rest on the EDGX Book where the Member receiving the report attempted to execute against that resting order within an Exchange-determined amount of time (not to exceed 1 millisecond) after receipt of the first attempt to execute against the resting order or quote and within an Exchange-determined amount of time (not to exceed 100 microseconds) before receipt of the first attempt to execute against the resting order or quote. For example, if a Member sends in a marketable order, but an order resting on the Exchange order book was subsequently executed, the Missed Liquidity Report can assist the Member in determining by how much time that order missed an execution. The Missed Liquidity Report includes the following data elements for orders and quotes: (1) Message Type; (2) Date; (3) Recipient Member ID; (4) Session Sub ID; (5) Clearing Identifier; (6) Client Identifier; (7) Trade Condition; (8) Auction ID; (8) Symbol; (9) Cboe Order ID; (10) Execution ID; (11) Exchange System Timestamps for orders, quotes, and cancels; (12) Matching Unit Number; (13) Queued; (14) Port Type; and (15) Aggressor Order Type. No specific information about resting orders on the Exchange book will be provided. Enhancements As noted above, the Exchange now seeks to update the Cboe Timestamping Service by adding additional data elements to the Missed Liquidity Report. Specifically, the Exchange seeks to enhance the Missed Liquidity Report to include COA and C-AIM events, as well as a new price field that includes each price level at which options orders were executed during an Auction, in addition to the Recipient Member's orders, modify message and quotes related to an Auction. Importantly, no other changes will be made to the Missed Liquidity Report, and aside from these proposed enhancements, the Missed Liquidity Report will remain as described above. As proposed, a Member's options orders, quotes and modify messages that are eligible to participate in an Auction will now appear in the Missed Liquidity Report. The Missed Liquidity Report will now show the Member the time details for their eligible options orders, quotes and modify messages for an Auction, as well as the time details for executions of other COA-eligible and C-AIM-eligible options orders resting on the Complex Order Book (``COB''), that the Member receiving the Missed Liquidity Report attempted to execute against within an Exchange-determined amount of time (not to exceed 1 millisecond) after receipt of the first attempt to execute against the resting options order and within an Exchange-determined amount of time (not to exceed 100 microseconds) before receipt of the first attempt to execute against the resting options order. For example, if a Member sends in a COA-eligible options order or a C-AIM-eligible options order (collectively, ``Auction Orders''), but a resting options order participating in the Auction was subsequently executed, the Missed Liquidity Report can assist the Member in determining by how much time their options order missed an execution. Additionally, for Auctions clearing across multiple price levels, the Missed Liquidity Report will now also include a new price field that shows each price level at which (i) the Auction Orders were executed during an Auction; and (ii) the Recipient Member's order, modify messages and quotes were at. This will enable a Member to see where their orders, modify messages, and quotes sat relative to the price levels at which other options orders executed in the Auction. Purpose The Exchange proposes introduce enhancements to the Cboe Timestamping Service, which is a market data service comprised of the Missed Liquidity Report, Missed Cancels Report and All Cancels Report. Specifically, the Exchange seeks to update the Missed Liquidity Report to now include Complex Order Auction (``COA'') events, as well as a new price field that, for records related to COA, includes each price of the subscribing Member's orders, modify messages, and quotes, as well as each price level at which options orders were executed during a COA. The Exchange is not proposing any enhancements to either the Missed Cancels Report or the All Cancels Report. Background Currently, the Cboe Timestamping Service provides timestamp information for orders, quotes and cancels for market participants. More specifically, the Cboe Timestamping Service reports provide various timestamps relating to the message lifecycle throughout the Exchange System. The reports are optional products that are available to all Members and Members may opt to choose any combination of reports or no reports at all. Corresponding fees are assessed based on the number of reports selected. Notably, the data included in these reports is based only on the data of the market participant that opts to subscribe to the reports (``Recipient Member'') and does not include information related to any Member other than the Recipient Member. The Exchange restricts all other market participants from receiving another market participant's data. Additionally, no report includes real-time market data. Rather, the reports contain only historical data from the prior trading day and are only available after the end of the trading day, generally on a T+1 basis. For example, if a Member sends in a marketable order, but an order resting on the Exchange order book was subsequently executed, the Missed Liquidity Report can assist the Member in determining by how much time that order missed an execution. Self-Regulatory Organizations; National Securities Clearing Corporation; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Enhance Automated Reasonability Checks for the Submission of ETF Creation and Exemption Transactions

1. Purpose The purpose of this proposed rule change is to amend the NSCC Rules to enhance NSCC's automated reasonability checks for the submission of ETF creation and redemption transactions by including authorized participants that are Members of NSCC in the reasonability check process and clarifying certain obligations of Index Receipt Agents and authorized participants with respect to this process. Specifically, NSCC proposes to modify the NSCC Rules to (i) include authorized participants in the ETF reasonability check process; (ii) clarify that Index Receipt Agents and authorized participants are required to subscribe to NSCC's designated communication method for pended transaction data and identify and regularly maintain contact persons authorized to receive notifications and review and confirm the validity of pended transactions (such persons being ``authorized approvers''); and (iii) clarify requirements concerning the form, manner and timing for such confirmations. The proposed rule change is discussed in detail below. Background ETFs (referred to as ``index receipts'' in the NSCC Rules) are marketable securities that track stock indices, commodities, bonds, or baskets of assets. ETFs are listed on exchanges and are traded throughout the trading day. Shares of ETFs are created and redeemed in the primary market and are traded on listed exchanges in the secondary market. Each share of an ETF represents an undivided interest in the underlying assets of the ETF. NSCC facilitates central counterparty clearing and settlement of the creation and redemption of ETF shares in the primary market as well as clearing of ETF trades in the secondary market. The participants in the ETF primary market typically consist of the issuers of ETFs (``ETF Sponsors''), custodian banks (``ETF Agents,'' also referred to as ``Index Receipt Agents'' in the NSCC Rules), and brokers/dealers that have agreements directly with ETF Sponsors to allow the brokers/dealers to place orders for the creation and redemption of ETF shares (referred to as ``authorized participants''). Both ETF Agents and authorized participants are Members of NSCC. In general, authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares from the ETF Sponsors in blocks called ``creation units.'' An authorized participant that purchases a creation unit of ETF shares delivers a ``basket'' of securities and other assets to the ETF Agent and then receives the creation unit of ETF shares in return for those assets. The redemption process is the reverse of the creation process; the authorized participant redeems a creation unit of ETF shares in exchange for a basket of securities and other assets. These creation and redemption baskets are referred to as ``trading baskets.'' NSCC supports the creation and redemption of ETFs on both an ``in-kind'' and ``cash-only'' basis. Under the NSCC Rules, Index Receipt Agents are authorized to submit creation and redemption transaction data on behalf of other Members (i.e., authorized participants). The obligations of the Member reflected in such transaction data are deemed to have been confirmed and acknowledged by each Member or designated by the Index Receipt Agent as a party thereto and to have been adopted by such Member. Pursuant to Section F.2. of Procedure II of the NSCC Rules, NSCC performs automated reasonability checks on creation and redemption transaction data submitted by Index Receipt Agents and may pend any transaction data that exceeds certain thresholds established by NSCC. If NSCC pends any transaction data that exceeds the pre- established thresholds, NSCC notifies the Index Receipt Agent of any transaction data that NSCC has pended. The Index Receipt Agent must then provide confirmation, in the form and within the timeframe required by NSCC, that such pended transaction data should be accepted by NSCC. If the Index Receipt Agent fails to provide such confirmation, the pended transaction data is rejected. NSCC's current reasonability checks pend any transactions (i) with a total settlement value of $15 billion or greater or (ii) when the variance between the net asset value (``NAV'') on the order and the prior day's closing NAV is 98% or greater in either direction. Pursuant to the NSCC Rules, NSCC has the authority to adjust thresholds from time to time and may consider feedback from its Members or market conditions when considering adjustments to such thresholds. NSCC's ETF reasonability checks were designed to provide ETF Agents with an opportunity to review and confirm certain potentially misvalued transactions that have been submitted to NSCC before such transactions are processed by NSCC and before the potentially misvalued transactions would be able to have an impact on, for example, a Member's daily Clearing Fund requirements. NSCC is now proposing to enhance this process to further minimize the risk of processing misvalued or erroneous transactions. 1. Purpose The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at Nasdaq Equity 7, Sections 115 and 130, to remove obsolete references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol. On October 22, 2026, the Exchange filed with the Commission a proposal, with immediate effectiveness, to abandon plans to deploy the CORE FIX order entry protocol. The Exchange now proposes to delete from its equities fee schedule (Nasdaq Equity 7) all references to CORE FIX, which had been added to the fee schedule in anticipation of testing and deploying CORE FIX. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to make the following changes: 1. In Equity 7, Section 115(f)(1), remove the reference and associated price for CORE FIX, including the tags to notes ``1'' and ``**'', as well as the corresponding notes ``1'' and ``**''. This rule established a fee of $575, per month, per port, for CORE FIX. a. Note ``1'' read ``Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX Ports. The Exchange shall offer users a 30-day waiver of the CORE FIX port fee for up to five newly added CORE FIX ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on the date when CORE FIX first becomes available on the Exchange, which such date the Exchange shall announce in an Equity Trader Alert.'' b. And Note ``**'' read ``Subject to Exchange Rule Equity 1, Section 1(a)(19), the first five Night Session CORE FIX ports ordered for an MPID will be provided without charge. Beginning with the sixth Night Session CORE FIX port ordered for the same MPID, the Exchange will assess the standard fee otherwise applicable to CORE FIX ports under this Section 115(g) of Rule Equity 7.'' 2. In Equity 7, Section 130(d)(1)(B), remove the tag to note ``1'', as well as the corresponding note ``1''. This rule establishes, in relevant part, a fee of $300 per port, per month, for subscribers that conduct tests of their access protocol connections through the Nasdaq Testing Facility. Note ``1'' read ``Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX NTF Ports. The Exchange shall offer subscribers a 30-day waiver of the $300 NTF fee in this paragraph (d)(1)(B) of Section 130 for up to five newly added CORE FIX NTF ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on a date to be specified by the Exchange in an Equity Trader Alert.'' 3. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange's proposed changes to its schedule of credits are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In NetCoalition v. Securities and Exchange Commission, the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: ``[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .'' The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system ``has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.'' Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of incentives and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds. Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal represents a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase its liquidity and market share relative to its competitors. The Exchange's proposal is also reasonable, equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it removes obsolete references to CORE FIX and related temporary waiver language from the fee schedule. The Exchange has determined not to deploy CORE FIX, and the provisions proposed for deletion therefore would not govern an active protocol or an active fee offering. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system ``has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.'' Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of rebates and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds. Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal represents a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase its liquidity and market share relative to its competitors. The Exchange's proposal is also reasonable, equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it removes obsolete references to CORE FIX and related temporary waiver language from the fee schedule. The Exchange has determined not to deploy CORE FIX, and the provisions proposed for deletion therefore would not govern an active protocol or an active fee offering. Removing references to the CORE FIX production port fee, CORE FIX disaster recovery port fee, CORE FIX Testing Facility ports, and related temporary waiver language will not change the availability, pricing, or functionality of any service currently used by members, and will apply equally to all market participants. Instead, the proposal will make Equity 7, Section 3 easier to navigate, understand, and administer by eliminating text that could otherwise create confusion regarding unavailable protocol functionality, obsolete fees, and waiver language that will not apply. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 5, Series of Options Contracts Open for Trading, to revise certain strike intervals applicable to options on ETFs that are more than one month and less than nine months from expiration and to make related organizational changes to that section. The Exchange also proposes to amend the rule text related to Qualifying Securities in Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 (Short Term Options Series Program). Background Currently, Options 4, Section 5(d) provides that, except as otherwise provided in the Supplementary Material thereto, the interval between strike prices of series of options on individual stocks will be: (1) $2.50 or greater where the strike price is $25.00 or less; (2) $5.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $25.00; and (3) $10.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $200.00. Current Section 5(e) separately provides that options on SPDR S&P 500 ETF (``SPY''), iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (``IVV''), PowerShares QQQ Trust (``QQQ''), iShares Russell 2000 Index Fund (``IWM''), SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (``DIA''), and SPDR[supreg] Gold Trust (``GLD'') (collectively ``enumerated ETFs''), may be listed at $1 or greater intervals; Section 5(e) applies only to the aforementioned ETFs. The unlettered paragraph of Section 5(d) generally provides $1 or greater intervals for ETFs where the strike price is $200 or less and $5.00 or greater intervals where the strike price is greater than $200. Additionally, currently Supplementary Material .03(e) to Options 4, Section 5 permits the Exchange to open for trading Short Term Option Series at strike price intervals of (i) $0.50 or greater where the strike price is less than $100, and $1 or greater where the strike price is between $100 and $150 for all option classes that participate in the Short Term Options Series Program; (ii) $0.50 for option classes that trade in one dollar increments and are in the Short Term Option Series Program; or (iii) $2.50 or greater where the strike price is above $150. Today, the Exchange's listing rules at Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 permit the listing of additional expirations on eligible individual stocks or Exchange-Traded Fund Shares that meet certain criteria on a quarterly basis (``Qualifying Securities''). Specifically, as measured on the last day of the prior calendar quarter, an underlying security must have either (A) a market capitalization greater than 700 billion dollars for an individual stock, based on the closing price, or (B) Assets under Management (``AUM'') greater than 50 billion dollars (under (B)(i)) or greater than 25 billion dollars (under (B)(ii)) for an Exchange-Traded Fund Share, based on net asset value (``NAV''). Further, eligible individual stocks or ETFs must have monthly options volume, as measured by sides traded in the last month preceding the quarter end, of greater than 10 million options, or greater than 5 million options for an Exchange- Traded Fund Share that qualified under (B)(ii) of the Qualifying Securities criteria; must have a position limit of at least 250,000 contracts; and must participate in the Penny Interval Program. Each calendar quarter, the Exchange applies the Qualifying Securities criteria to individual stocks and ETFs to determine eligibility for the following quarter as a Qualifying Security. Beginning on the second trading day in the first month of each calendar quarter, the market capitalization of individual stocks is calculated based on the closing price established on the primary exchange on the last trading day of the prior calendar quarter and the AUM for ETFs is calculated based on the NAV established on the primary exchange on the last trading day of the prior calendar quarter. Proposal At this time, the Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 5, Series of Options Contracts Open for Trading. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to incorporate current Options 4, Section 5(e) into Options 4, Section 5(d) and remove the ``(e)'' designation so that it becomes unlettered text within Section 5(d). Under the proposal, the general $1-or-greater interval for ETFs where the strike price is $200 or less and the $5.00-or-greater interval where the strike price is greater than $200, as well as the $1-or-greater interval for the enumerated ETFs, will remain unchanged, except that ETF Qualifying Securities may be listed at $0.50 or greater intervals where the strike price is less than $100, as described below. The Exchange also proposes to amend current Options 4, Section 5(e) to remove the clause ``Notwithstanding any other provision regarding the interval of strike prices of series of options on Exchange-Traded Fund Shares in this Rule,'' and to amend certain ETF names to reflect the current name. So that the first sentence of the proposed unlettered paragraph states, ``The interval of strike prices on SPDR S&P 500 ETF (``SPY''), iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (``IVV''), PowerShares QQQ Trust (``QQQ''), iShares Russell 2000 Index Fund (``IWM''), the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (``DIA''), and SPDR[supreg] Gold Trust (``GLD'') options will be $1 or greater.'' Self-Regulatory Organizations: Long-Term Stock Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend LTSE Rule 3.291

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291, Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities, to conform the rule so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. The Exchange notes that this filing is based on a proposal recently submitted by FINRA, and approved by the Commission, to amend FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others). Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act, the Exchange and FINRA entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the ``17d-2 Agreement''). The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules. The 17d-2 Agreement included a certification by the Exchange that states that the requirements contained in certain Exchange rules are identical to, or substantially similar to, certain FINRA rules that have been identified as comparable. To conform to comparable FINRA rules for purposes of the 17d-2 Agreement, the Exchange proposes conforming the text of LTSE Rule 3.291 so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. Currently, LTSE Rule 3.291 is excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it is not identical, or substantially similar, to FINRA Rule 3220. Current LTSE Rule 3.291 prohibits a Member or person associated with a Member from directly or indirectly, giving or permitting to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of one hundred dollars per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. FINRA Rule 3220 currently prohibits gifts in excess of $300.00, where the gift or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. Unlike FINRA Rule 3220, current LTSE Rule 3.291 does not include provisions covering: supervision and record keeping requirements; an exclusion for payments made pursuant to bona fide, written employment contracts; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts; de minimis gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to a Member's associated persons or individual retail customers. LTSE Rule 3.291 was, therefore, excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it was not identical or substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. To harmonize its rules with FINRA, the Exchange proposes to conform the rule text of LTSE Rule 3.291 to text that is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 so that it may be incorporated into the 17d-2 Agreement in its entirety. The Exchange believes that these changes will help to avoid confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing LTSE Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed changes to LTSE Rule 3.291 are designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate LTSE Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, LTSE Rule 3.291 would equally apply to Exchange-only Members as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when a Member or person associated with a Member gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer. First, the Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291(a) to increase the gift limit from $100 to $300 per individual per year. FINRA stated that the current gift limit of $100 has been in place since 1992. FINRA increased the gift limit from $100 to $300 to account for past inflation since 1992 and to account for expected future inflation for approximately ten years, thereby reducing the frequency of future upward adjustments to account for inflation. Consistent with FINRA's determination, the Exchange believes that a $300 gift limit would continue to permit the exchange of business courtesies while helping to guard against excessiveness, and reasonably reflects changes to purchasing power due to inflation since the gift limit was last raised in 1992 as well as approximately ten years of expected future inflation. Second, the Exchange proposes to add a new paragraph (d) to LTSE Rule 3.291 that would authorize FINRA staff to conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of LTSE Rule 3.291 for good cause shown, provided that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. Specifically, the Exchange proposes that pursuant to LTSE Rule Series 9.600 (Procedures for Exemptions), FINRA staff, for good cause shown after taking into consideration all relevant factors, may conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of this Rule to the extent that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; NYSE Texas, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Adopt New Rule 8a To Provide for the Listing of Acquisition Companies
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; NYSE Texas, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Adopt New Rule 8a To Provide for the Listing of Acquisition Companies

1. Purpose In 2025, the Exchange reincorporated in the State of Texas and was re-named NYSE Texas, Inc. In 2026, the Exchange amended certain of its initial and continued listing standards to facilitate new listings on the Exchange. The Exchange now proposes to adopt new Rule 8a to provide for the listing of Acquisition Companies. In order to qualify for listing a class of common stock on the Exchange, an issuer must meet one of four initial listing standards contained in Rule 8. An Acquisition Company would can qualify for listing pursuant to initial listing standards 3 or 4 as initial listing standards 1 and 2 require prior operating history. To account for the differences between a standard operating company and an Acquisition Company, the Exchange proposes to adopt the following additional listing criteria for Acquisition Companies: a. At least 90% of the gross proceeds from the initial public offering and any concurrent sale by an Acquisition Company of equity securities must be deposited in a trust account maintained by an independent trustee, an escrow account maintained by an ``insured depository institution,'' as that term is defined in Section 3(c)(2) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, or in a separate bank account established by a registered broker or dealer (collectively, a ``deposit account''). b. Within 36 months of the effectiveness of its initial public offering registration statement, or such shorter period that the Acquisition Company specifies in its registration statement, the Acquisition Company must complete one or more business combinations having an aggregate fair market value of at least 80% of the value of the deposit account (excluding any deferred underwriter's fees and taxes payable on the income earned on the deposit account) at the time of the agreement to enter into the initial combination. c. Until the Acquisition Company has satisfied the condition in paragraph (b) above, each business combination must be approved by a majority of the Acquisition Company's independent directors. d. Until the Acquisition Company has satisfied the condition in paragraph (b) above, if the Acquisition Company holds a shareholder vote on a business combination for which the Acquisition Company must file and furnish a proxy or information statement subject to Regulation 14A or 14C under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 in advance of the shareholder meeting, the business combination must be approved by a majority of the shares of common stock voting at the meeting at which the combination is being considered. If a shareholder vote on the business combination is held, public shareholders voting against a business combination must have the right to convert their shares of common stock into a pro rata share of the aggregate amount then in the deposit account (net of taxes payable and amounts distributed to management for working capital purposes) if the business combination is approved and consummated. An Acquisition Company may establish a limit (set no lower than 10% of the shares sold in the initial public offering) as to the maximum number of shares with respect to which any shareholder, together with any affiliate of such shareholder or any person with whom such shareholder is acting as a ``group'' (as such term is used in Sections 13(d) and 14(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934), may exercise such conversion rights. For purposes of this paragraph (d), public shareholder excludes officers and directors of the company, the company's sponsor, the founding shareholders of the company, any family member or affiliate of any of the foregoing persons, and other concentrated holdings of 10% or more. For purposes of the proposed rule, ``family member'' means a person's spouse, parents, children and siblings, whether by blood, marriage or adoption, or anyone residing in such person's home. e. Until the Acquisition Company has satisfied the condition in paragraph (b) above, if a shareholder vote on the business combination is not held for which the Acquisition Company must file and furnish a proxy or information statement subject to Regulation 14A or 14C under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the Acquisition Company must provide all shareholders with the opportunity to redeem all their shares for cash equal to their pro rata share of the aggregate amount then in the deposit account (net of taxes payable and amounts distributed to management for working capital purposes), pursuant to Rule 13e-4 and Regulation 14E under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which regulate issuer tender offers. The Acquisition Company must file tender offer documents with the Securities and Exchange Commission containing substantially the same financial and other information about the business combination and the redemption rights as would be required under Regulation 14A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which regulates the solicitation of proxies. Until the Acquisition Company completes a business combination where all conditions in paragraph (b) above are met, the company must notify the Exchange on the appropriate form about each proposed business combination. Following each business combination, the combined company must meet the requirements for initial listing. If the Acquisition Company does not meet the requirements for initial listing following a business combination or does not comply with one of the requirements set forth above, the Exchange shall commence delisting proceedings under Rule 4(c) to delist the company's securities. The Acquisition Company shall not be eligible to follow the procedures to cure deficiencies outlined in Interpretation and Policy .01 to Rule 17A. If the Acquisition Company is subject to delisting due to a failure to comply with paragraph (b) above, the Exchange will immediately suspend trading in the company's securities at the time of commencement of delisting proceedings and trading in the Acquisition Company's securities will remain suspended

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Adopt FINRA Rule 1240.03 (Senior Leader Regulatory Element Interim Program) To Establish an Interim Program of Regulatory Element Continuing Education
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Adopt FINRA Rule 1240.03 (Senior Leader Regulatory Element Interim Program) To Establish an Interim Program of Regulatory Element Continuing Education

1. Purpose Pursuant to Rule 1240, registered persons of member firms are required to complete CE that consists of two mandatory programs, a Regulatory Element and a Firm Element. Regulatory Element CE, which is administered by FINRA, focuses on regulatory requirements and industry standards. Firm Element CE is provided by each member firm to its registered persons and focuses on the firm's securities products, services and strategies, its policies, and industry trends. FINRA has received a variety of suggestions from member firms and industry groups regarding changes to the Regulatory Element CE requirement for senior leaders (e.g., chief executive officer, chief financial officer). FINRA received similar suggestions regarding this topic in response to Regulatory Notice 25-07. FINRA believes that Regulatory Element CE provides individuals with valuable training on recent developments in regulatory requirements and industry standards, and as such, CE is appropriate for all registered persons, including senior leaders. FINRA, however, recognizes that senior leaders at member firms may realize greater benefit from Regulatory Element CE training that draws from the annual Regulatory Element content but is tailored to their unique roles at a member firm. Senior leaders may engage with FINRA rules differently than frontline representatives and principals because they have broader visibility and responsibilities across their member firm, and often its broader organizational structure. FINRA believes that Regulatory Element CE content for such leaders therefore may be more effective if it covers the information addressed in the various Regulatory Element CE learning plans but presents the information from a broader, firm- wide perspective. Such content could focus on firm risks, control systems, approaches to pressure-test firm capabilities and vulnerabilities, and similar enterprise-level considerations. Therefore, FINRA is proposing to adopt Rule 1240.03 to establish a Senior Leader Regulatory Element Interim Program (``Interim Program''). The proposed Interim Program, which would operate for just over two full years, would provide member firms with the option for their senior leaders to complete continuing education covering Regulatory Element topics, such as new and amended rules and regulatory trends, framed from the perspective of their unique roles and responsibilities at a member firm. Under the proposed Interim Program, participating senior leaders would continue to be required to take this continuing education on an annual basis, but the content of the training and the method of delivery would be different. For the proposed Interim Program, FINRA would, as it does today, develop the Regulatory Element CE training materials on an annual basis. In developing these training materials, FINRA would consider the annual learning plan topics assigned to each registration category. However, rather than limiting the content to the specific registration categories the senior leaders hold, the materials would cover content across all registration categories. FINRA would present significant rule changes, key regulatory developments and other Regulatory Element topics from the unique organizational vantage point of senior leaders. The materials would remain consistent with the core objectives of Regulatory Element CE but would be tailored to that senior leader audience. FINRA would make the Regulatory Element CE training materials available to those member firms that elect to participate in the proposed Interim Program. Unlike the manner in which Regulatory Element CE is currently delivered, the chief compliance officer (``CCO'') or other senior compliance officer at a member firm participating in the proposed Interim Program would provide the training to the participating senior leaders (including any participating senior leaders of affiliated entities). Further, the CCO or other senior compliance officer would have the discretion to supplement the training materials to provide the most relevant and effective training for the senior leaders at his or her firm; there would be no requirement to create or deliver any additional material specific to the registration(s) that any of the senior leaders hold. A senior leader who participates in the proposed Interim Program would be required to certify that he or she has completed the Regulatory Element CE training, and the member firm would need to retain such certification for at least three years. In addition, CCOs of member firms that choose to participate in the proposed Interim Program would be required to identify to FINRA those senior leaders who completed the training and demonstrated proficiency in the subject matter covered by the educational material. Senior leaders who participate in the proposed Interim Program and successfully complete the training would satisfy their annual Regulatory Element CE under Rule 1240. Those senior leaders who do not participate in the proposed Interim Program would be required to complete the Regulatory Element CE courses assigned by FINRA, as they do today. As noted, FINRA is proposing to establish the Interim Program for a period of just over two full years. The proposed Interim Program would be voluntary and no member firm would be required to participate. While the proposed Interim Program is in place, FINRA would evaluate the demand for the proposed Interim Program and whether it is meeting the goals of Regulatory Element CE for senior leaders at member firms. If no further action is taken, the proposed Interim Program would automatically sunset at the end of the designated period. FINRA has filed the proposed rule change for immediate effectiveness and has requested that the Commission waive the requirement that the proposed rule change not become operative for 30 days after the date of filing so FINRA can implement the proposed rule change immediately. 2. Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq PHLX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Equity 8A Regarding Information Circular Requirements

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to eliminate the requirement that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange as provided in Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A). The Exchange also proposes to amend Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(1) to add express cross-references to General 9, Section 10 (Recommendations to Customers (Suitability)) and Equity 2, Section 20 (Customer Disclosures). The Exchange also proposes to amend Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B)(ii) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities, not later than the time a confirmation of the first transaction in such series is delivered to such purchaser. The Exchange also proposes to renumber Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B) through (E) as Section 5(a)(2)(A) through (D), respectively. The Exchange also proposes a number of updates in Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2), specifically to replace the obsolete cross-reference to any ``UTP Security'' with a more general reference to any ``security'' and to update the cross-reference to ``UTP Exchange Traded Product'' in Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2). The proposal is similar to a proposal that Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (``Cboe BZX'') filed with the Commission. Equity 8A, Section 5 governs the trading of UTP Exchange Traded Products on the Exchange--securities listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (``UTP''). Under current Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally mirrors the information circular issued by the listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the new exchange traded product; (b) the Exchange rules that will apply to the new exchange traded product; and (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indices. The Exchange proposes to delete Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A) in its entirety. The information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes. The Exchange's issuance of a separate, duplicative circular therefore serves no independent investor protection function. The Exchange also proposes to amend Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(1) to add express cross-references to General 9, Section 10 (Recommendations to Customers (Suitability)) and Equity 2, Section 20 (Customer Disclosures). Current Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A) does not reference the recommendations to customers/suitability provisions addressed by General 9, Section 10 and the risk of trading outside of regular trading hours addressed by Equity 2, Section 20, but the Exchange is proposing to add these explicit cross-references in Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(1) to highlight their visibility in the context of UTP Exchange Traded Products, consistent with Cboe BZX's proposal. These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross-references are intended to make the applicable framework explicit in the context of UTP Exchange Traded Products. General 9, Section 10 independently requires Members to ensure that any recommendation of a UTP Exchange Traded Product is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, a standing obligation that applies regardless of whether the Exchange has issued a product-specific information circular. Similarly, Equity 2, Section 20 independently requires Members to provide customers with a written disclosure of the risks of trading outside of regular trading hours before accepting any order for execution outside of regular trading hours, a standing obligation not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product- specific information circular. Because Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange satisfies the notification obligation under Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B), deletion of Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(A) necessitates a conforming amendment to Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B). The Exchange proposes to amend Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B)(ii) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities, not later than the time a confirmation of the first transaction in such series is delivered to such purchaser. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Exchange Traded Product, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the information circular provided by the listing exchange or open-ended management company issuing such securities in the same manner and to the same effect. The Exchange also proposes to renumber existing Equity 8A, Section 5(a)(2)(B) through (E) as Section 5(a)(2)(A) through (D), respectively. title: IEX Options FIX Order Entry and Drop Copy Specification Update
raw_text:
IEX Options FIX Order Entry and Drop Copy Specification Update
Category: Trading; Alert 2026-040
IEX Options has updated its IEX Options FIX Specification to v1.04, reflecting a change to the Execution Report “Partial and Full Fills” message and “Trade Bust / Correction” message published on both FIX Order Entry and FIX Drop Copy Sessions. The expected value for the ContraBroker field on these messages has been updated. Specifically, if the counterparty to a trade does not provide a CMTA value on their order, the ContraBroker field will now be populated with “0” instead of being space-filled. Previous ContraBroker Field Description: Contra party clearing number of CMTA. Will match value populated on contra order if provided. Otherwise space-filled . 5 digits. New ContraBroker Field Description: Contra party clearing number of CMTA. Will match value populated on contra order if provided. Otherwise populated with “0”. Up to 5 digits. This change will be reflected in the IEX Options production system beginning Tuesday, November 10. Additional Resources IEX Options FIX Specification Contact Information Please contact the IEX Options Market Operations team with any questions at optionsmktops@iextrading.com. About The Investors Exchange Investors’ Exchange LLC (IEX Exchange or IEX) is a national securities exchange designed to provide superior execution quality and set a new standard for trading. IEX operates in both equities (IEX Equities) and options (IEX Options). Since launching in 2016, IEX Equities has grown to be one of the largest exchange operators globally, by notional value traded. In October 2026, IEX launched IEX Options, a new U.S. options exchange that brings its suite of order protection innovations designed to better address the needs of market makers and drive better outcomes for end investors. To learn more visit iex.io .

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq Texas, LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposal To Amend Equity 4 To Remove All References to the CORE FIX Order Entry Protocol
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq Texas, LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposal To Amend Equity 4 To Remove All References to the CORE FIX Order Entry Protocol

1. Purpose In September 2025 the Exchange added CORE FIX to its rulebook in Equity 4, in anticipation of making this new order entry protocol available to Exchange Participants in October of 2025. In December 2025 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the first quarter of 2026. In March 2026 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the end of 2026. In spite of its best efforts, the Exchange has been unable to generate interest in CORE FIX among Exchange Participants. Therefore, rather than deploy an order entry protocol that Participants are not even interested in testing, the Exchange proposes to abandon its plans to deploy CORE FIX. This will allow the Exchange to better allocate its technological development resources. The Exchange notes that it will continue to offer all the order entry protocols that are currently available and operative on the Exchange--namely, OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX. The Exchange proposes to eliminate all references to CORE FIX that are currently present in Equity 4. Specifically, these references are found in Rules 4702 (Order Types), 4703 (Order Attributes), and 4757 (Book Processing). 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade because it will ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the order entry protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX, which the Exchange will not deploy, will avoid confusion among Participants and other market participants regarding the protocols available for order entry. The proposed rule change will not alter the operation of the Exchange's market, the treatment of orders, or the rights or obligations of Participants; the Exchange will continue to offer the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols. Accordingly, the proposal will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and will protect investors and the public interest by providing clear and accurate information concerning the Exchange's order entry protocols. B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issue; instead, its purpose is to ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX will not deprive any Participant of an available order entry protocol, because CORE FIX has not been deployed on the Exchange. Participants will continue to be able to choose among the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols based on their trading needs. Accordingly, the proposal will not impose any burden on competition, either among Exchange Participants or between the Exchange and other trading venues. C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others No written comments were either solicited or received. III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved. IV. Solicitation of Comments Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods: Electronic Comments Use the Commission's internet comment form (https://www.sec.gov/rules/sro.shtml); or Send an email to [email protected]. Please include file number SR-NasdaqTX-2026-051 on the subject line. Paper Comments Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NasdaqTX-2026-051. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (https://www.sec.gov/rules/sro.shtml). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. In March 2026 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the end of 2026. In spite of its best efforts, the Exchange has been unable to generate interest in CORE FIX among Exchange Participants. Therefore, rather than deploy an order entry protocol that Participants are not even interested in testing, the Exchange proposes to abandon its plans to deploy CORE FIX. This will allow the Exchange to better allocate its technological development resources. The Exchange notes that it will continue to offer all the order entry protocols that are currently available and operative on the Exchange--namely, OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX. The Exchange proposes to eliminate all references to CORE FIX that are currently present in Equity 4. Specifically, these references are found in Rules 4120 (Limit Up-Limit Down Plan and Trading Halts), 4702 (Order Types), 4703 (Order Attributes), and 4757 (Book Processing). Finally, the Exchange proposes to use this filing to make a technical correction to Equity 4, Rule 4120(b)(1)(C)(ii)(e)(2). That rule provides that following a regulatory halt pursuant to the Limit Up-Limit Down Mechanism, ``limit-priced orders entered via the OUCH or CORE FIX protocols which are not assigned a Managed Pegging, Discretionary, or Reserve Order Attribute, the order shall be repriced upon entry only if the Price Bands are such that the price of the limit-priced interest to buy (sell) would be above (below) the Upper (Lower) Price Band.'' The reference to CORE FIX in that rule will be deleted as part of this filing. But the Exchange also wishes to correct this rule by adding the FLITE protocol, alongside the OUCH protocol. This is to reflect current Exchange functionality. In other words, the Exchange currently applies this rule to limit-priced orders entered via the OUCH of FLITE protocols, even though the FLITE protocol is not currently included in this rule. The Exchange proposes to correct this oversight in this filing. Therefore, pursuant to this filing, Equity 4, Rule 4120(b)(1)(C)(ii)(e)(2) will state that ``limit-priced orders entered via the OUCH or FLITE protocols which are not assigned a Managed Pegging, Discretionary, or Reserve Order Attribute, the order shall be repriced upon entry only if the Price Bands are such that the price of the limit-priced interest to buy (sell) would be above (below) the Upper (Lower) Price Band.'' 2. The proposed technical correction to Rule 4120(b)(1)(C)(ii)(e)(2) will likewise make the rule text accurately reflect current Exchange functionality by adding the FLITE protocol alongside the OUCH protocol. The proposed rule change will not alter the operation of the Exchange's market, the treatment of orders, or the rights or obligations of Participants; the Exchange will continue to offer the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols. Accordingly, the proposal will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and will protect investors and the public interest by providing clear and accurate information concerning the Exchange's order entry protocols and order handling functionality. B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issue; instead, its purpose is to ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange and the functionality currently provided through those protocols.
